1:
The date is reckoned from the turn of the year, and the reckoning is agreed. Gill takes "after the year was expired" with the Targum as meaning at the end of the year, which closed with the month Adar, or February, so that what follows belongs to the spring. Wesley has the old year ended and the next begun, and explains the phrase about the going forth of kings from the ground rather than the calendar: spring is when the soil is fit for the march of soldiers and brings forth provision for man and beast. Clarke sets it about a year after the Syrian war already described and calls the spring the most proper season for military operations, adding Calmet's suggestion that two campaigns were made in the year, one in autumn and one in spring, the winter being in many respects inconvenient and the summer too hot. Ellicott renders the opening literally, as the margin does, at the return of the year, and reads it as pointing back to the close of the Syrian campaign (2 Samuel 10:14).

Who went out and who stayed behind is reconstructed in some detail. Ellicott has Joab spend the winter, the rainy season, at Jerusalem and now return to Ammon, and explains the division of forces: David had evidently hurried his own campaign against Hadarezer to prevent the junction of his foes, Joab having probably been sent out at first with only a small force to hold the Ammonites in check; when David's operations closed quickly and successfully he came back to Jerusalem and the bulk of the army was sent on to join Joab. Henry reads the same movement as generalship and gives David the credit of it before taking it away again. Having routed the Ammonite army in the field, as soon as the season permitted he sent more forces to waste the country and further avenge the quarrel of his ambassadors; Rabbah, their metropolis, made a stand and held out a great while, and to that city Joab laid close siege. It was during that siege, Henry notes, that David fell into this sin, which is why the beauty of the action cannot be viewed with the pleasure his earlier achievements allow.

One textual curiosity attaches to the phrase itself. Ellicott points out that by the insertion of a letter the Hebrew text as written reads not "when kings go forth" but "when angels," or messengers, "go forth," a reading corrected in the margin.

What was done to the Ammonites in the field is softened by comparison with the parallel. Ellicott notes that where this verse says the army destroyed the children of Ammon, the Chronicles explain the phrase as wasting the country of the children of Ammon (1 Chronicles 20:1), and he fills in the practice behind it: after the custom of ancient warfare, while the main body besieged Rabbah, foraging parties were sent out to lay the country waste and cut off any stragglers, as the spoiling companies of an earlier campaign had done (1 Samuel 13:17). The last clause of the verse is where Henry and Wesley converge, and both read it as the hinge of the chapter. When David should have been abroad with his army in the field, fighting the battles of the LORD, he devolved the care upon others and himself tarried still at Jerusalem — and to the Syrian war he had gone in person. Had he been at his post at the head of his forces, each of them says in nearly the same words, he would have been out of the way of this temptation. When we are out of the way of our duty, Henry adds, we are in the way of temptation.
2:
The hour is fixed carefully, because the sightline depends on it. Gill puts it some time in the afternoon as the sun began to decline, not in the dusk, since in the dusk the object could not have been seen so distinctly. Clarke has David reposing on the roof to enjoy the breeze, the noonday being too hot for business, and notes that this is still a constant custom on the flat-roofed houses of the East. Ellicott makes it the siesta customary in Oriental countries: late in the afternoon David rose from his couch and walked on the roof of his palace, which in the cool of the day was the pleasantest part of an eastern house. Wesley adds only that he had lain and slept there some time, and draws the moral in a phrase Henry uses as well — the bed of sloth often proves the bed of lust.

What he could see from there Ellicott works out from the ground. The palace stood on the height of Mount Zion and looked down upon the open courts of the houses in the lower city, and in one of those courts David saw a beautiful woman bathing. It was common in such courts to keep a basin of water, and the place was probably entirely concealed from every point of observation except the roof of the palace, from which no harm was suspected.

Whether the woman was blameless is where Clarke argues against himself. He first presses the suspicion hard: how could any woman of delicacy expose herself where she could be so fully and openly viewed, did she not know she was at least in view of the king's terrace, and was there no design in all this? — a question he clinches with a line of Latin verse about the girl who flees to the willows but wants to be seen first. Then he supplies the exculpation himself. In a Bengal town pools of water are to be seen everywhere, and women may be seen bathing in them morning and evening and carrying water home, so that David might have seen Bathsheba with no blame attaching to her. On the washing itself the readings agree. Wesley puts her in a bath in her garden, probably cleansing from some ceremonial pollution; Clarke points forward to the next verses as showing that the washing came at the termination of a particular period.

Two of them stand back from the verse to measure the fall. Keil and Delitzsch call it a turning-point not only in the inner life of the great king but in the history of his reign: hitherto David had kept free from the grosser sins and had shown only such infirmities as simulation and prevarication, which clung to all the saints of the Old Covenant and were hardly regarded as sins at that stage of religious culture, though God never left them unpunished but visited them on his servants with chastisements of various kinds. Among the unacknowledged sins God tolerated because of the hardness of Israel's heart they place polygamy, which encouraged licentiousness and the tendency to sensual excess, and against which only a weak barrier had been raised by the warning given to Israelite kings against taking many wives (Deuteronomy 17:17). Ellicott locates the cause differently, in the long course of uninterrupted prosperity and power which had somewhat intoxicated David and thrown him off his guard. It is no part of the plan of Scripture, he adds, to cover up or excuse the sins of even its greatest heroes and saints; this sin was followed by the deepest repentance and by divine forgiveness, and yet its punishment overclouded all the remaining years of David's life. The fall, on a word of Augustine's that Ellicott passes on, should put upon their guard those who have not fallen and save from despair those who have.
3:
The enquiry is treated as the decisive act, not the sight that preceded it. Gill allows that David may at first have meant no harm by it — he asked who she was, what she was called, and whether she had a husband, and if she had none he very probably intended to wed her, designing at that point to go no further and to nothing dishonourable — but Gill will not let the enquiry pass as innocent on that account: it would have been better for him not to have inquired at all, and to have endeavoured to stifle the motions raised in him at the sight of her. Wesley puts the same judgement without the concession. Instead of suppressing the desire which the sight of his eyes had kindled, David seeks rather to feed it, and asks first after her identity so that, should she prove single, he might make her either his wife or his concubine. Henry reads the intention as genuinely open at that moment: perhaps David meant only, if she proved free, to take her to wife as he had taken several, and if she were another man's to have no design upon her at all.

The answer comes back in a form two of them pause over. Keil and Delitzsch note that the verb is singular — he, that is, the messenger, said, or taken indefinitely, they said — and that the interrogative which opens the reply is used here, as it often is, in the sense of an affirmation: it is indeed so.

Both proper names in that reply stand otherwise in the parallel passage, and the handling of the discrepancy varies. Keil and Delitzsch lay the spellings side by side: where this verse has Bathsheba the daughter of Eliam, the Chronicles read Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel (1 Chronicles 3:5), and they judge the first of those two forms correct and original on the evidence of the later history of the succession (1 Kings 1:11). On the paternal one they decline to rule. Eliam and Ammiel signify the same thing and differ only in the order of their two elements, and which came first it is impossible to determine. Ellicott treats such inversion as a frequent variation among Scripture names and translates the pair accordingly, God's people and the people of God. Clarke presses further than either, rendering them the people of my God and the God of my people, and hearing in the words themselves the terms of the covenant — I will be your God, we will be thy people.

The husband's standing is what makes the verse damning rather than merely informative. Ellicott notes that Uriah's name stands in the roll of David's thirty chief heroes (2 Samuel 23:39), and that the whole story represents him as a brave and noble-minded soldier. David had by now given rein to his guilty passion so far that the knowledge of Bathsheba's being a married woman, and the wife of one of his own chief warriors, does not check him.
4:
The sending and the taking are read closely, because the words could carry either persuasion or force, and everyone who comments decides for persuasion. Keil and Delitzsch say there is no intimation whatever that David brought Bathsheba into his palace through craft or violence, but rather that she came at his request without any hesitation and offered no resistance to his desires. Ellicott agrees that the phrase does not imply the use of violence. Clarke puts it as an absence of evidence — we hear nothing of her reluctance, and there is nothing to show she was taken by force. Wesley states it plainly, out of her own house into his palace, not by force but by persuasion. Gill, who elsewhere spares David nothing, here records only that the messengers went to invite her to the palace.

That agreement raises the question of her share in the guilt, and the answers are harder on her than the narrative is. Keil and Delitzsch conclude that Bathsheba is therefore not to be regarded as free from blame: the very act of bathing in the uncovered court of a house in the heart of the city, into which anyone might look down from the roofs standing on higher ground, does not say much for her feminine modesty, even if it was done with no ulterior purpose, as some have supposed. Ellicott reaches the same verdict by another road, judging from her part in the struggle over the succession that she was a woman of little discretion (1 Kings 2:13), and he supposes her perhaps flattered by the approach of the king. Yet he will not let the comparison end there: David, he says, was nevertheless a far greater offender. Keil and Delitzsch frame the sin itself by the proverb about desire, that when lust has conceived it brings forth sin (James 1:15), and the information that the beautiful woman was married proved not enough to stifle the sensual desires that had arisen in David's soul. Wesley draws the slope rather than the act — see how all the way to sin is downhill, and when men begin they cannot soon stop themselves.

The clause about her purifying is given two quite different functions. Ellicott takes it as a correction of the tense and a point of law: read "and she was", not "for she was"; under the Law she remained unclean until the evening, so she stayed in the palace until that hour — scrupulous in this detail, he observes, while conscious of a capital crime and a high offence against God. Clarke reads it instead as physiology, pointing forward from the washing of the previous verse to this one as marking the time at which conception is most likely, and he makes the woman's conceiving the proof of his reading.

What the conception meant to each of them was not a child but a sentence. Gill says the sin would now be discovered, and shame and disgrace, or worse, must follow. Keil and Delitzsch read her message as an appeal to David to take the steps necessary to avert the consequences, since the law required that both adulterer and adulteress be put to death (Leviticus 20:10); Ellicott says the same in a sentence, that she sent word because her sin must now become known and the Law condemned both parties to die. The three words of her message are allowed to stand without comment by any of them.
6:
The order travels a long way, and the man it fetches is no ordinary soldier. Gill measures the distance, reporting on Bunting's authority that Rabbah, where Joab lay with the army, stood sixty-four miles from Jerusalem. Keil and Delitzsch fix Uriah's rank from the later roll: he was one of the gibborim, David's mighty men, and therefore held some post of command in the army — though they reject outright the further claim, made by Josephus, that he was Joab's armour-bearer or aide-de-camp, for which there is no historical foundation. Henry adds the one circumstance that makes the summons plausible at all: Uriah had by now been some weeks away from his wife, making the campaign in the country of the Ammonites, and did not intend to return until it ended.

Why David wanted him home Henry works out as the avoidance of two separate dangers, both of them lethal. The wife's condition would in time bring the hidden works of darkness to light, and when Uriah discovered how he had been wronged, and by whom, two things might be looked for. He might prosecute his wife under the law and have her stoned, jealousy being the rage of a man, and especially of a man of honour, who will not spare in the day of vengeance (Proverbs 6:34); Henry thinks Bathsheba foresaw exactly this when she sent her message, which was an intimation that David was now bound to protect her, and judges it likely that without such a promise beforehand she would never have consented to him at all — hope of impunity being a great encouragement to iniquity. Or, having no legal remedy against a king, he might take his revenge another way and raise a rebellion; and there have been kings, Henry notes, who by provocations of just this kind given to powerful subjects have lost their crowns.

The design that answers both dangers is set out most compactly by Ellicott, in three steps. By calling for Uriah and treating him with marked consideration David thought to establish a friendly feeling on his part; by then sending him home to his wife he meant to have it supposed that the child begotten in adultery was Uriah's own; and by that supposition the crime would be covered. Henry puts the same thing in a phrase — David endeavours to father the child upon Uriah himself, and therefore sends for him home to stay a night or two with his wife.

The cover story is the weakest part of it, and two of them say so. Keil and Delitzsch will only say that Uriah was sent for upon some pretext or other, and that the question David put to him on arrival, how it fared with Joab and the people and the war, was probably that pretext. Henry presses the point harder. David pretends a more than ordinary concern for his army at the one moment when the army was the least thing in his thoughts; and had he not had another turn to serve, a messenger of far less figure than Uriah would have been enough to bring him a report of the state of the war. That a commanding officer should be recalled sixty-four miles to deliver what any courier could have carried is, on Henry's reading, where the pretence shows through.
7:
Uriah reports to the palace before he goes anywhere else. Gill notes that he came to David first, before his own house, wanting to know what the king's special business with him was; Keil and Delitzsch record the three questions he was asked — how Joab did, how the people did, how the war prospered — and then the dismissal. The order to go down and wash his feet is read in two layers. Keil and Delitzsch supply the custom: the Israelites washed their feet on returning home from work or from a journey, as a way of taking refreshment and rest, and the going down is literal, from the palace on Mount Zion to the lower city where Uriah's house stood. Gill, Clarke and Wesley all read the king's purpose through it. Gill says the refreshment was to prepare him for bed, which was what David wanted to get him to. Wesley has David not doubting he would there converse with his wife and so cover their sin and shame. Clarke spells out the whole calculation — that the child now conceived should pass for Uriah's, the honour of Bathsheba be screened and the king's own crime concealed. Clarke adds a limit worth keeping: at this point David had no design of murdering Uriah, nor of taking Bathsheba to wife.

The dish that follows him out is a smaller touch with the same purpose. Ellicott renders the phrase literally as a present, notes that the same word serves for the portions Joseph sent from his own table (Genesis 43:34), and takes it for some choice dish sent by the king to a guest he wished to honour. Clarke's verdict on it is four words: all this was artfully contrived.

Where Uriah spent the night instead is located three ways, all of them close together. Keil and Delitzsch put him before or at the door of the king's house, meaning in the court of the palace or in an adjoining building where the court servants lived. Ellicott prefers the guard chamber at the palace entrance (1 Kings 14:27). Clarke says one of the apartments or niches in the court, and offers a modern parallel, that in Bengal servants commonly sleep on the verandahs or porches facing their master's house. Gill reconstructs the evening: Uriah, well known to the bodyguards posted to watch the palace by night, very likely fell into conversation with them, one and another inquiring after friends in the army, and being weary he lay down among them and slept.

Whether he stayed away on purpose is the one real disagreement in these verses. Keil and Delitzsch say his suspicions had been aroused, the connection between his wife and David perhaps not having remained altogether a secret, so that it may have reached his ears as soon as he arrived in Jerusalem. Ellicott denies the need for any such supposition: it is quite unnecessary to suppose Uriah suspected anything, his conduct and language being simply those of a brave, frank, generous-hearted soldier. Henry reports both views and then settles it with an argument from a later verse — some think he was informed of his wife's attendance at court and therefore would not go near her, but had he harboured any suspicion of that kind he would surely have opened the letter David afterwards sent by his hand to Joab. What Henry puts in place of suspicion is providence, which put the resolution into his heart and held him to it so that David's sin should be discovered; and Wesley says the same in a line, that he did this by the secret direction of God's wise providence, which would bring the sin to light.
10:
David hears of the failure in the morning — from those who carried the dish, Gill suggests, or from the guards Uriah had slept among — and puts his question as a kindness. Keil and Delitzsch render it closely: didst thou not come from the way, that is, from a journey, and why then didst thou not go down, as men generally do on returning from one? Clarke and Wesley both fill in the courteous surface of it. Clarke has David say that keeping watch or guard is no duty of his, that he has come off a journey and needs rest and refreshment; Wesley has him disclaim the service altogether — wearied with hard travel as thou art, I neither expected nor desired that thou shouldst attend upon my person or keep the watch.

The answer is given in full by Keil and Delitzsch and glossed by them in one phrase: to sit or sojourn in huts amounts practically to being encamped in the open field. What Uriah meant, on their reading, is that while the ark — that is, the LORD with the ark — and all Israel were engaged in conflict with the enemies of God and of his kingdom, and were therefore quartered in the open country, it did not become him to go home to eat and drink and lie with his wife. The refusal is sealed with an oath on the king's own life and soul: I will not do this thing. Gill records it simply as his apology for the conduct.

Whether the ark had actually gone to the war is a point on which they divide, and the division is not trivial, since Uriah's whole argument leans on it. Clarke takes the words at face value — it appears therefore that they had taken the ark with them to battle. Wesley agrees and calls the practice usual, the ark being carried for the army's encouragement and direction. Ellicott grants the custom and marks what it cost to keep it: notwithstanding the experience of the ark's capture by the Philistines in the days of Eli (1 Samuel 4:11), it still seems to have been carried out in war as a symbol of God's presence and a pledge of his favour (1 Samuel 14:18). Henry alone leaves the question open, allowing that the ark was in a tent either way — at home in the tent David had pitched for it, or abroad with Joab in the camp — and declining to say which. Ellicott adds a point of date rather than place: the separate naming of Israel and Judah here is no evidence of a late hand, those two parts of the nation having already been divided, and even hostile, in the early years of David's reign.

On the quality of the refusal there is no division at all. Clarke calls it the answer of a brave, generous and disinterested man, and reads its sense as a vow — I will not indulge myself while all my fellow soldiers are exposed to hardship, and the ark of the LORD itself in danger; then he puts again the question he had raised earlier, whether Uriah really had no suspicion of what had been done in his absence. Wesley draws the principle out: when God's people are in a doubtful and dangerous condition it becomes a man to sympathize with them and to abstain even from lawful delights. Henry sets the resolution against the statute it exceeds — the law required that when the host went out against the enemy a man should then in a special manner keep himself from every wicked thing (Deuteronomy 23:9) — and the comparison is the sting: Uriah outdid that law, and David violated it.
12:
Ellicott says what Uriah's answer should have accomplished and did not. It ought to have stung David to the quick, but his conscience was so deadened by the sin already committed that its only effect was to drive him to a baser means of concealment still — and that baser means is the supper.

Keil and Delitzsch state the hope behind it, that in such a state Uriah would give up his resolution and go home; Clarke the same, that being off his guard he would hasten down to his house. Ellicott declines to comment on the attempt and remarks only on what it proved — that the soldier's resolve was strong enough to govern his conduct even in that almost irresponsible condition. Henry refuses to let the act pass as a stratagem merely. It is a very wicked thing, upon any design whatsoever, to make a person drunk, and woe to him that does it (Habakkuk 2:15): robbing a man of his reason is worse than robbing him of his money, and drawing him into sin worse than drawing him into any trouble whatsoever.
14:
The failure of one crime is what produces the next, and all four of them say so. Gill has David informed that Uriah slept with the servants rather than going home, upon which Satan put it into his heart to take this wicked and cruel method. Keil and Delitzsch put it as a calculation: his plan frustrated by Uriah's obstinacy, the king resolved upon a fresh and greater crime. Henry traces the reasoning — with Uriah dead there could be no prosecution, there being no prosecutor, and Bathsheba might be his own for ever. Adulteries have often occasioned murders, Henry adds, and one wickedness must be covered and secured with another; the beginnings of sin are therefore to be dreaded, for who knows where they will end?

Two of them measure the distance David has travelled. Keil and Delitzsch see how deep a soul may fall when it turns from God and from the guidance of his grace: this same David, who in the days of his persecution would not resort even to plausible means to defend himself, was now not ashamed of the greatest crimes to cover his sin. Henry asks it as two memories. Is this the man whose heart smote him because he had cut off the skirt of Saul's robe? Is this he that executed judgment and justice to all his people? The change he lays to the war fleshly lusts wage against the soul, which blinks the eyes, hardens the heart, sears the conscience and strips away all sense of honour and justice (Proverbs 6:32).

The method is read as a choice among methods. Henry sets it beside two others the history offers — not as Absalom killed Amnon, by commanding servants to assassinate him, nor as Ahab killed Naboth, by suborning witnesses, but by exposure to the enemy, a way that perhaps would not look so odious to conscience or to the world, because soldiers expose themselves as a matter of course. None of which, Henry insists, saves it from being wilful murder of malice prepense. Concealment was wanted because, as with the eye of the adulterer, so the hand of the murderer seeks the dark (Job 24:15): David slew Goliath publicly and gloried in it, and had to slay Uriah in secret, being ashamed of it — who would do a thing he dare not own?

That the warrant travelled in its victim's own hand is the detail each of them fastens on. Clarke calls it the sum of treachery and villany, David making this most noble man the carrier of letters that prescribed his own murder. Ellicott adds the double use made of him: the brave soldier bears his own death-warrant, and his known valour for his king becomes the very means of his destruction. Ellicott notes too what the letter withheld — no reason was given to Joab, who as a loyal and somewhat unscrupulous general obeys without question. Henry counts the aggravations. The deed was deliberate: David took time over it, wrote it out, could have countermanded it, and persisted. And sending it by Uriah's own hand was base and barbarous beyond the rest, making the man accessory to his own death — a paradox, Henry thinks, that David could bear such malice toward the one man he still trusted with sealed orders he must not read.

Clarke alone fetches a parallel from outside Scripture and then refuses it. Having rehearsed at length the tale of Bellerophon, falsely accused by a queen whose advances he had declined and sent on with letters asking for his death, Clarke answers those who have thought it a fabulous formation out of this history: for his own part he scarcely sees any correspondence beyond the single circumstance that both men carried the letters containing their own condemnation. The proverb it bequeathed, for carrying one's own condemnation, is what he keeps.
15:
The order has two clauses, and the difference between them is what the commentary turns on. Keil and Delitzsch render the whole of it closely — set ye Uriah opposite to the strongest contest, and then turn away behind him, that he may be smitten and die — so that the first clause places the man and the second withdraws his support. Gill records the verse with no gloss at all beyond its function, that these were the orders given to Joab.

Ellicott is the one who notices that only half the instruction was obeyed. The direction to retire from him was not carried out, and he offers two guesses why: perhaps Joab judged that it would make the stratagem too evident, or perhaps it was simply impracticable in the field. The consequence of that disobedience he states without softening it. Because the troops around Uriah stood instead of withdrawing, others were killed along with him, and a larger blood-guiltiness fell upon David than the letter had bargained for — the king's crime grew in the execution beyond what the king had written.

Whether Joab understood what he was being asked to do is left deliberately open by Keil and Delitzsch, and their caution runs against the natural inference. The literal fulfilment of the command, they insist, does not warrant us in assuming that Joab suspected how the matter stood, or that he had heard any rumour of it. A general unaccustomed to sparing human life would carry out such an order faithfully without needing to know the reason for it; and on their reading his obedience settles the question of his knowledge in neither direction.

Wesley's comment is on the writer rather than the letter. So far is David from repenting, he says, that he seeks to cover one sin with another — the murder is not a lapse following the adultery but a measure taken to protect it, and the one crime is now in the service of the other. On the sentence itself Wesley is as blunt as the text: David has sinned, therefore Uriah must die.
16:
The verb governing Joab's survey is given three senses, and the choice decides what he was doing. Ellicott takes it to mean watched, or blockaded. The Targum, as Gill reports, reads it as besieged. Gill's own gloss makes it reconnaissance, Joab observing where the city's greatest strength lay and where it was best defended. Ellicott turns that survey into a deliberate arrangement: in the operations of the siege Joab so disposed some of his forces as to invite a sally from the city under circumstances in which the sally would succeed. He finds the proof of how far forward they were pushed in the messenger's own later report, that Uriah's party had been sent near enough to come within reach of the archers on the wall.

Whose valour the verse means is a smaller question with a sharp edge. Keil and Delitzsch read the clause as placing Uriah just where Joab knew there were brave men, and the brave men are the defenders inside the city, not the company Uriah led — the position was dangerous because of who would come out of it. Gill reads the sally the same way: the men of the city made their sortie, as Joab expected they would, once his troops appeared at that part of the wall where the valiant men were posted.

What happened next is where Clarke and Ellicott part company over a matter of fact. Clarke says the withdrawal took place: Uriah was led to the attack of a place defended by valiant men, and in the heat of the assault Joab and his men retired from this brave soldier, who cheerfully gave up his life for his king and his country. Ellicott, commenting on the letter itself, had held that this part of David's orders was never carried out at all, and that the casualties among the others are the evidence of it. The narrative does not settle the point, since it records only that some of the people of the servants of David fell, and that Uriah the Hittite died also.

Keil and Delitzsch use the obedience to raise the question of Joab's motive and then decline the obvious answer. The literal fulfilment of the king's command does not warrant the assumption that Joab suspected how the matter stood or had heard any rumour of it. A general unaccustomed to sparing human life would be a faithful servant to his lord in such a point — and their explanation of why he would be faithful is not loyalty but exchange: so that his own interests might be served another time.
18:
The report is sent off at once and comes with a script. Gill notes that Joab despatched his messengers as soon as Uriah was killed; Keil and Delitzsch give the instructions in full, and the shape of them is a conditional. The man is to tell the whole business of the war to the end; then, if the king's anger should rise and he should ask why they advanced so near the city to fight, and whether they did not know that men would shoot from the wall, and who it was that smote Abimelech the son of Jerubbosheth, and did not a woman throw down a millstone from the wall so that he died in Thebez, and why then went ye so nigh the wall — then, and only then, the messenger is to say that thy servant Uriah the Hittite has perished. Gill puts the same thing as stagecraft: the direction was for the close of the narrative, and was to be used according as the man should observe the king's countenance to be, wrath being legible there or in his words.

What Joab expected the anger to be about is agreed. Keil and Delitzsch have him assume that David might be angry at the losses, or at any rate express displeasure that Joab had sacrificed a number of warriors by imprudently approaching close to the wall. Ellicott calls it anticipating David's anger at his apparent rashness. Clarke supplies a motive behind the precaution that neither of the others does: it is likely Joab had by some indiscretion suffered loss about this time, and he contrived to get rid of the odium by connecting that loss with a death he knew would be pleasing to the king.

The old precedent is traced out for its own sake. Keil and Delitzsch identify the man behind both names — Jerubbosheth being Jerubbaal, that is, Gideon (Judges 6:32) — and refer the millstone to its place in the earlier history (Judges 9:53). Gill explains the alteration of the name itself: Baal, one part of it, was the name of an idol, and was sometimes replaced by Bosheth or Besheth, a word signifying shame, the idol being a shameful one. Both Ellicott and Henry draw the same lesson from the citation, that the reference shows how familiar the people were with their own past; Henry presses it further, observing that the book of Judges was likely already published as part of the sacred history in Samuel's time, and that even the soldiers were conversant with their bibles and could readily quote the scripture story and apply it as a warning against running upon attempts they knew had proved fatal.

Whether the messenger could see through his errand is the one point of real disagreement. Ellicott says he could not: mentioning Uriah's death was not likely to awaken any suspicion in him, since it would appear rather as an effort on Joab's part to shift the blame from himself onto Uriah as the leader of the assaulting party. Henry says the opposite, that the instruction gave too broad an intimation to the messenger, and through him to others, that David would be secretly pleased to hear it — for murder will out, and when men do such base things they must expect to be upbraided with them even by their inferiors. Ellicott adds one observation that cuts against the whole elaborate plan: the messenger appears to have told everything in one breath, so that David never had the opportunity to express the displeasure the script was written to manage.
23:
The messenger does not keep to his orders. Keil and Delitzsch observe that he brought David all the information Joab had charged him with, but so condensed it as to mention Uriah's death at the same time rather than holding it back for the moment of the king's anger: the men of the city became strong against them and came out into the field, they prevailed against them as far as the gate, the archers shot from the wall, some of the king's servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite is dead also. Gill, who takes the report verse by verse, fills in the hardware — arrows out of their bows or stones out of their engines — and explains how the range was closed: the Israelites followed the sallying party so near to the gate that they came within reach of the shot from the wall.

David's reply is heard four different ways, and the readings run from composure to hypocrisy. Keil and Delitzsch describe him receiving with apparent composure the intelligence he was naturally so anxious to hear, and render his message back to Joab closely — let not this thing depress thee, for the sword devours thus and thus; keep on with the battle against the city and destroy it. They gloss the idiom as a refusal of a particular judgement rather than a general consolation: do not look upon this affair as evil, that is, as disastrous. The parting word to the messenger they render literally, strengthen him, put courage into him.

Ellicott hears something more than encouragement in the wording. The reply is ostensibly meant to steady Joab on the ground that the mishap was a mere accident of war, and yet it is couched in such language as to imply a special regret for the loss of this particular man — one as well as another meaning, on his paraphrase, that though Uriah was a brave hero whom they could ill spare, the fortune of war does not let us choose who shall fall, and that notwithstanding the loss Joab should go on with a good heart.

Clarke and Henry allow no such reading. Clarke calls it abominable hypocrisy outright: David knew perfectly well that Uriah's death was no chance-medley, the man having been thrust upon the edge of the sword by his own order. Henry hears secret satisfaction under the composure. David is not displeased and therefore tells Joab not to be; he blames nothing in the conduct of the assault and does not think they did wrong to approach so near the wall, because all is well now that Uriah is out of the way. That point gained, he can make light of the loss and turn it off with an excuse — the sword devours one as well as another, a chance of war, nothing more common. And Henry catches the contradiction in the last clause of the order: David tells Joab to make the battle stronger against the city while he himself, by this sin, was weakening it and provoking God to blast the whole undertaking.
26:
How the widow learned of it Gill answers from David's interest rather than from the custom of the army. The news was soon sent her by the king, and Gill thinks it very probable she knew nothing of the plot to take away her husband's life; what is certain is that David chose to have the death published abroad as soon as possible, the more effectually to hide his own sin. The verse itself Keil and Delitzsch pass over without a word of comment, letting it stand as the narrative gives it.

Whether the grief was genuine is where Clarke commits himself and nobody contradicts him. The whole of her conduct, he judges, indicates that she observed the form without feeling the power of sorrow; and he states the exchange she had made with a dry contempt — she lost a captain and got a king for her spouse, which must have been deep affliction indeed. He seals the verdict with a couplet of Latin verse, which he renders himself: she shed reluctant tears, and forced out groans from a joyful heart.

How long the mourning lasted is not stated, and Ellicott says so before estimating it. The usual term was seven days, on the two precedents he cites, one from the patriarchal history and one from the burial of Saul and his sons (1 Samuel 31:13); and although a widow's mourning may well have run somewhat longer than the common period, it was doubtless, under these circumstances, made as short as was consistent with decency. Henry puts the same conclusion as an act rather than an estimate: she submitted to the ceremony of mourning for her husband for as short a time as custom would admit, and then David took her into his house as his wife.

The brevity is therefore read by both of them as evidence. Neither treats the shortened mourning as grief cut short by circumstance; both treat it as a term calculated down to the minimum that would pass — the one reckoning by what decency required, the other by what custom would admit.
27:
The haste of the marriage is measured against two standards. Gill reckons the seven days at an end, or sooner, then applies a later rule: David did not stay the ninety days from the husband's death that the Jews afterwards enjoined, so that it might be known to whom a widow's child belonged — and for not waiting that term Abarbinel charges him with an additional sin. Clarke and Wesley both read the speed as concealment: the hurried marriage was intended on both sides to cover the pregnancy, and the thing could not admit of longer delay, lest the too early birth of the child discover the sin.

The birth, when it comes, is read as the mechanism by which the concealment failed. Henry puts it briefly: Uriah's revenge was prevented by his death, but the birth of the child so soon after the marriage published the crime. Ellicott makes that the answer to a harder question. Several months passed in which David's conscience had not brought him to a sense of what he had done, nor had Nathan yet been sent. Why was he left so long unconvicted? One obvious reason, Ellicott answers, is that the sin might be fastened upon him openly, beyond all possibility of denial, by the birth of the child. Wesley draws from the same interval a conclusion about human nature rather than divine timing: that David continued impenitent for divers months, notwithstanding his frequent attendance upon God's ordinances, is an eminent instance of the corruption of man's nature, the deceitfulness of sin, and the judgment of God in punishing one sin by delivering a man up to another.

Ellicott will not grant that the silence of those months was that of a quiet mind. David was through all of it not only civil ruler but head of the theocracy, whose psalms carried the people's devotion; and however hardened he appears in passing from crime to crime, it is scarcely possible his conscience was not at work meantime, oppressing him with that sense of unconfessed sin which prepared him at last for the prophet's visit.

On the closing clause they do not divide. Clarke says it was necessary to add it, lest the splendour of David's former virtues should let anyone suppose his crimes were looked on indulgently by the God of purity and justice: sorely he sinned and sorely did he suffer, sowing one grain of sweet and reaping a long harvest of calamity and woe. Henry gathers the series under one verdict — the adultery, the falsehood, the murder and this marriage at last were all displeasing to the LORD, who sees and hates sin in his own people; and the nearer any are to God in profession the more displeasing their sins are, there being in them more ingratitude and reproach than in the sins of others. Let none, he concludes, encourage themselves in sin by David's example.

Clarke alone turns the chapter into an argument for the book that contains it. He calls it an illustrious proof of the truth of the sacred writings, and puts the case as a question: who that intended to deceive, by trumping up a religion he meant to father on the purity of God, would have inserted such an account of one of its most zealous advocates and brightest ornaments? God alone, whose character is impartiality, has done it, to show that his religion will stand independently of the conduct of its professors. He adds that those who have taken pains to varnish David's conduct here, whatever their ingenuity, write otherwise than the inspired penman did. His own apportioning of blame he gives in four verdicts — he pities David, fallen from great eminence; venerates Uriah; detests Joab as a ruffian and not a soldier, a pander to the vices of his monarch; and thinks meanly of Bathsheba, whom he judges first in the transgression.
